items.title: L7: Writing a briefing for a senior reader
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: communicating and influencing; GOV.UK guidance on writing for policy audiences
items.body:
A briefing helps a senior person make a decision or get ready for a meeting. They may read it between meetings, so it must work in two minutes. Start with the purpose and the 'so what': why the reader is getting this and what you want from them. A common structure is: purpose and recommendation, then the key facts, then the main risks, then next steps and any deadline. Put the detail in an annex that the reader can skip.

Lead with the answer, not the history. A paragraph that begins 'In 2019 the department...' pushes the point out of sight. Say 'We recommend extending the contract by six months because...', then give the reasons in order of importance. Limit yourself to what the reader needs for the decision, and cut what you only know.

State the confidence level. Say what is known, what is estimated and what is unknown, and do not hide uncertainty. If the figure is a forecast, say so. Compare figures with something meaningful, such as last year or the target, because 4,200 cases means little on its own.

Use headings, short paragraphs and a clear 'ask'. Spell out acronyms on first use. Include a contact for questions and say who has cleared the content, for example the legal or finance team.

Be impartial. A briefing should set out options fairly, even when you recommend one. If the reader will meet a stakeholder, add handling points: what the stakeholder is likely to ask, the lines the reader can use, and what must not be said. Check every number against the source before it goes up.

Mark the briefing with the right classification and send it only to the people who need it.

questions.prompt: What should come first in a briefing for a busy director?

options.text: The purpose and your recommendation
The methodology behind the figures
A full history of the policy
A list of everyone consulted

questions.hint: A senior reader needs the answer and the ask before any background.

questions.prompt: A draft briefing begins 'In 2019 the department introduced a pilot scheme...'. What is the main problem?

options.text: It is written in the active voice
It refers to a year rather than a financial year
The point is buried in history before the reader learns what is needed
It refers to a year rather than a financial year, which will confuse readers who work with budgets

questions.hint: Opening with background delays the recommendation the reader needs.

questions.prompt: Where should detailed tables and methodology usually go?

options.text: In the opening paragraph
In the subject line of the email
In an annex that the reader can skip
In the middle of the recommendation

questions.hint: Detail supports the case but should not hold up the main message.

questions.prompt: A briefing says 'Case numbers were 4,200 last quarter.' How could it be improved for the reader?

options.text: Compare the figure with something meaningful, such as the previous quarter or the target
Replace the figure with a percentage only
Give the number in words, and add the exact time that the data was extracted from the system
Add the exact time the data was extracted

questions.hint: A number is hard to interpret without a comparison.

questions.prompt: The figures in your briefing include a forecast. How should you present it?

options.text: Say clearly that it is a forecast and how confident you are in it
Present it like the actual figures so the briefing looks consistent
Leave it out because forecasts are always unreliable
Put it in a footnote so it does not distract from the main message

questions.hint: Readers must be able to tell fact from estimate to judge the risk.

questions.prompt: You recommend option B but option A has real merits. How should a briefing handle this?

options.text: Set out the options fairly and then explain why you recommend B
Describe A negatively so the choice looks obvious
Leave A out so the decision is straightforward
List A and B in a table without a recommendation

questions.hint: Impartial options help the reader decide and show you have considered alternatives.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of 'handling points' in a briefing for a meeting with a stakeholder?

options.text: To replace the recommendation with talking points
To summarise the stakeholder's background, past roles and recent public statements in detail
To tell the reader what they might be asked, what lines to take and what not to say
To record the attendees' dietary requirements

questions.hint: Handling points prepare the reader for the conversation.

questions.prompt: Which is the best opening for a briefing that asks the minister to approve a six-month extension?

options.text: Decision needed by Friday 14 March: we recommend extending the contract by six months.
The contract was signed in 2021 and has run for three years.
I am pleased to submit the following for your consideration.
This briefing gives a full background on the contract, its history and the suppliers who bid for it.

questions.hint: The ask, the deadline and the recommendation should appear immediately.

questions.prompt: Before a briefing goes to the director, what check is essential?

options.text: The briefing is at least two pages
Every number is checked against its source and the content is cleared by those responsible, such as finance or legal
The text is formatted in bold so key words stand out
A copy has been sent to the press office

questions.hint: Accuracy and clearance protect the department's credibility.

items.title: L7: Writing a submission with options and a recommendation
items.source: Civil Service Code; Managing Public Money (HM Treasury); Cabinet Office guidance on policy advice
items.body:
A submission is a formal piece of advice sent to a senior official or minister so they can decide something. Layouts vary between departments, but most follow the same logic. It starts with the issue and the decision you need, gives your recommendation, sets out the background briefly, discusses the options and their pros and cons, covers the risks and implications (such as financial, legal and communications), and finishes with next steps and timing.

The most important part is the decision requested. Write it as a clear sentence the reader can agree to, such as 'Please agree to option 2 by 14 March so that the contract can be signed before the existing one ends.' If there is a deadline, say why it matters.

Options should be genuinely different and fairly described. Include the 'do nothing' option as a baseline where it is realistic. For each option, give the cost, the benefits, the risks and any legal limits. Do not present a weak option only to make your preferred choice look good.

Under the Civil Service Code, officials must act with integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Advice should be accurate and evidence-based, and it should not be changed to please the reader. If the evidence points to a politically unwelcome conclusion, say so. Equally, you must not mislead or hold back relevant information.

Where public money is involved, Managing Public Money sets out principles such as regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility. A submission with a spending proposal should show the cost and value for money and have finance clearance where needed.

Cover the practical risks, a communications line and the next steps. Keep it to the length the department expects, usually a few pages with the detail in annexes.

questions.prompt: What is the most important part of a submission?

options.text: A quotation from the Civil Service Code
The list of everyone in the policy team
A full chronology of past events and every consultation held along the way
A clear statement of the decision requested and your recommendation

questions.hint: A submission exists so that the reader can make a decision.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a well-written 'ask' in a submission?

options.text: Option 2 may be a good approach.
Please agree to option 2 by 14 March so the contract can be signed before the current one ends.
It is hoped that a decision can be reached in due course.
We would welcome your thoughts on the options below, ideally before the end of the month if that is convenient.

questions.hint: A clear ask includes the choice, the date and the reason for the date.

questions.prompt: Why include a 'do nothing' option in an options section?

options.text: It sets a baseline so the reader can see what the other options change
It shows that the team has not yet made up its mind about which option to prefer
It is required by the Civil Service Code
It is the safest recommendation in every case

questions.hint: A realistic baseline makes the effects of other options visible.

questions.prompt: You prefer option C, but you know options A and B are better in cost. How should you handle this?

options.text: Remove A and B so that the minister has no alternative
Leave out the costs of A and B
Present all three options fairly, including the costs, and explain why C is recommended despite the cost
Describe A and B as unrealistic without evidence

questions.hint: Objectivity and honesty require full and fair information.

questions.prompt: Evidence suggests a policy will have a smaller effect than a minister hopes. What does the Civil Service Code expect?

options.text: Soften the findings so that the minister is not disappointed
Report the evidence accurately, even if it is unwelcome
Present only the most positive study
Wait until the minister asks before mentioning it

questions.hint: Honesty and objectivity mean giving advice based on evidence.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the core values in the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Efficiency
Integrity
Loyalty to the political party in power
Confidentiality at all costs

questions.hint: The Code lists integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality as the four core values.

questions.prompt: Which principle of Managing Public Money covers whether spending has Parliament's authority and is within the rules?

options.text: Feasibility
Efficiency
Regularity
Propriety

questions.hint: Regularity means spending complies with the legal authority and rules; propriety concerns standards of conduct.

questions.prompt: What should a submission with a spending proposal usually have before it goes to the minister?

options.text: Finance clearance and a clear value-for-money case
A signed letter from the supplier
A copy of the supplier's marketing brochure
Approval from the press office and a quotation from the supplier

questions.hint: Spending advice should be cleared by finance colleagues and show value for money.

questions.prompt: A minister's office asks for the deadline to be moved because it is inconvenient, but the contract expires on 31 March. What should the submission do?

options.text: Leave the date vague so there is no pressure
Explain what the deadline is, why it matters and what happens if it is missed
Remove the deadline from the submission, since it is only the department's own date
Change the date without comment

questions.hint: The reader needs the consequence of missing a deadline to decide.

items.title: L7: Responding to an MP or a representative
items.source: Data Protection Act 2018; ICO guidance on disclosing personal data to MPs and other representatives; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
items.body:
Members of Parliament often write to departments on behalf of people in their constituencies. A reply to an MP is a reply on behalf of the department, so it should be accurate, polite, in plain English and on time. Most departments have target times for answering MPs and ministerial correspondence, so log the letter at once and check how long you have.

Check what is being asked. Many MPs' letters contain several issues, so make a list and answer each one. If you cannot answer, explain why and say what you will do. Do not simply repeat the standard line. Where a policy applies, explain it and how it applies to the person's circumstances.

Data protection matters. In many cases a department can share a constituent's personal data with an MP who is acting for them, because the Data Protection Act 2018 has a condition for elected representatives. Even so, check that the MP is really acting for that person, and take extra care with sensitive information such as health data. If you are unsure, ask the data protection team. Do not give the MP more information than is needed to answer the enquiry.

A representative who is not an MP, such as a friend, relative, solicitor or charity worker, needs the person's authority. Ask for written consent unless the department's process says otherwise, and keep the authority on file.

If a complaint is still unresolved after the department's own complaint process, a constituent can ask an MP to refer it to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. The Ombudsman looks at whether there has been maladministration or poor service and can recommend a remedy.

Acknowledge the correspondence, reply within the target and record the reply.

questions.prompt: An MP writes about a constituent's claim and raises four separate issues. What is the best approach to the reply?

options.text: Phone the MP and avoid putting it in writing
Send the standard policy leaflet and offer to discuss the other issues by telephone later
Answer the most serious issue and say the others are being looked at
Answer each issue in turn and say what happens next on any you cannot resolve

questions.hint: A full reply shows each point was read and addressed.

questions.prompt: Why does a reply to an MP need particular care?

options.text: MPs can never receive personal data about their own constituents under any circumstances
It is a reply on behalf of the department and may be read by others or reported
MPs always need a reply within one working day
MPs' letters are exempt from the Civil Service Code

questions.hint: A reply speaks for the department, so accuracy and tone matter.

questions.prompt: An MP writes saying they are helping a constituent with a benefit claim. What is the right approach on sharing the constituent's data?

options.text: Send the whole case file to be safe
Usually it is possible to respond, but check the MP is acting for the constituent and share only what is needed
Reply only if the MP is a member of the governing party
Refuse all MP letters without the constituent's signature

questions.hint: The Data Protection Act 2018 has a condition for elected representatives, but proportionality still applies.

questions.prompt: A solicitor writes asking for details of a client's claim. What should you do first?

options.text: Send the details only if the claim is already closed
Check you hold written authority from the client
Ask the solicitor to phone you instead
Send the details because solicitors are trusted professionals

questions.hint: Third-party representatives need the individual's authority.

questions.prompt: When may a constituent ask their MP to refer a complaint to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman?

options.text: Only when the department refuses to reply
Only when the claim is worth more than £1,000
Before making any complaint to the department, so that the Ombudsman can deal with it first
When the complaint has not been resolved by the department's own complaints process

questions.hint: The department must have the chance to resolve it first.

questions.prompt: What does the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman examine?

options.text: Whether an official should be dismissed
Whether a department has complied with the FOI Act
Whether the minister's policy is right and whether Parliament should change the law
Whether there has been maladministration or poor service and what remedy is needed

questions.hint: The Ombudsman's remit is administrative fault and service failure, not policy merit.

questions.prompt: An MP's letter asks about a policy. The standard line does not answer the specific question. What should you do?

options.text: Hold the reply until the MP asks again
Address the specific question and explain how the policy applies to the case
Reply that the policy is a matter for ministers and that officials cannot comment on it
Send the standard line anyway

questions.hint: Repeating a generic line without engaging with the question frustrates the reader.

questions.prompt: What should be the first step when an MP's letter arrives?

options.text: File it until a supervisor has time
Forward it to all team members
Put it in the post tray
Log it and check the target date for reply

questions.hint: Early logging means deadlines are visible and the letter is not missed.

items.title: L7: Formal meetings: records, conflicts and Chatham House
items.source: Cabinet Office guidance on conflicts of interest; Chatham House Rule (Royal Institute of International Affairs); Civil Service Code
items.body:
Formal boards, panels and committees follow a standard order. Common items are apologies for absence, declarations of interest, minutes of the last meeting, matters arising, the main business, any other business and the date of the next meeting. A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for decisions to be valid. If the meeting is inquorate, it should not take binding decisions.

A declaration of interest is made when a member has a personal, financial or other interest that could affect, or appear to affect, their judgement. The chair decides what follows. Options include leaving the room for that item, taking part in the discussion without voting, or no action where the interest is minor. The minutes record the declaration and what was done. Failing to declare an interest can damage confidence in the decision even when the person acted fairly.

The Chatham House Rule applies to some discussions. Under it, participants are free to use the information they receive, but neither the identity nor the affiliation of the speaker or any other participant may be revealed. Minutes of such meetings record the points made but not who made them.

Decisions should be recorded with the reasons, so there is an audit trail. If a decision is challenged by judicial review or a complaint, good minutes show that relevant factors were considered and irrelevant ones were not. Draft minutes should be circulated promptly and checked by the chair.

Keep distinct the minutes (a record of the meeting) and the action log (a running list of who must do what). Keep sensitive material in an annex with limited circulation.

questions.prompt: In a formal meeting, what does 'quorum' mean?

options.text: The minimum number of members who must be present for decisions to be valid
The number of members who must vote in favour before any decision can be passed
The members who have declared an interest
The senior official who chairs the meeting

questions.hint: Without a quorum a meeting should not take binding decisions.

questions.prompt: A panel member's brother works for a company bidding for a contract on the agenda. What should the member do?

options.text: Leave the panel without telling anyone
Declare the interest at the start so the chair can decide how to handle it
Wait until the vote and then abstain without explaining the reason to anyone
Say nothing because the brother is not their employer

questions.hint: Declaring promptly lets the chair protect the integrity of the decision.

questions.prompt: Who decides what happens after a declaration of interest?

options.text: The most junior attendee
The chair
The member who declared it
The person who wrote the agenda

questions.hint: The chair decides whether the member stays, takes part or leaves the room.

questions.prompt: What should the minutes show about a declared interest?

options.text: Nothing, so as to protect the member's privacy
The financial details of the member's interest
Only the name of the member
That the interest was declared and what action was taken

questions.hint: The record shows transparency and how the conflict was managed.

questions.prompt: Under the Chatham House Rule, what can participants do with the information they receive?

options.text: Keep it confidential for 30 years
Use it only within their own organisation
Use it, but not reveal who said it or their affiliation
Publish it with the speaker's name provided that the meeting was not private

questions.hint: Information may be used freely, but sources stay anonymous.

questions.prompt: Minutes of a Chatham House meeting should record:

options.text: Each speaker's name, grade and employer so that the record is complete
Only the decisions and not the discussion
The points made without attributing them to named speakers
Exactly what each person said word for word

questions.hint: The rule protects identities, so the minutes must not reveal them.

questions.prompt: A meeting is inquorate. What is the right action?

options.text: Ask absent members to vote by text afterwards without recording it
Take the decisions anyway and record them as provisional
Do not take binding decisions, and note the position or reconvene
Count the minute-taker as a member

questions.hint: Decisions taken without a quorum can be invalid.

questions.prompt: Why is it important that minutes record the reasons for a decision?

options.text: They are legally required to be in verse
They give an audit trail that shows relevant factors were considered if the decision is challenged
They allow the chair to avoid answering questions
They make the minutes longer and more detailed

questions.hint: Evidence of reasoning helps defend a decision from challenge or review.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between minutes and an action log?

options.text: Minutes are a record of the meeting; the action log tracks who must do what and by when
Minutes record actions only; the log records decisions
The log is for the chair and the minutes are for the public
There is no difference as they are always the same document

questions.hint: Keeping them separate makes progress on actions easier to follow.

items.title: L7: Spreadsheets: INDEX and MATCH
items.source: Microsoft Support: INDEX and MATCH functions
items.body:
INDEX and MATCH together form a flexible alternative to VLOOKUP. MATCH finds the position of a value within a single row or column. INDEX returns the value at a given position in a range. Combined, MATCH supplies the position and INDEX fetches the result.

The syntax of MATCH is =MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]). Use 0 for an exact match. 1 (the default) finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value and needs ascending data. -1 finds the smallest value greater than or equal to it and needs descending data. If nothing matches, MATCH returns #N/A.

The syntax of INDEX is =INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]). For a single column you only need the row number. For a table, give both row and column numbers.

Suppose B2:B7 holds the offices Leeds, Cardiff, Belfast, Bristol, Glasgow and Norwich, and C2:C7 holds the number of staff: 45, 32, 28, 51, 39 and 24. Then =MATCH("Bristol",B2:B7,0) returns 4, as Bristol is the fourth item. =INDEX(C2:C7,4) returns 51. Combined, =INDEX(C2:C7,MATCH("Bristol",B2:B7,0)) returns 51. =INDEX(B2:C7,3,2) returns 28, the value in the third row and second column of the block.

The main advantages over VLOOKUP are that the result column can be to the left of the lookup column, and inserting or deleting columns does not break the formula, because it refers to ranges rather than a fixed column number.

For a two-way lookup, use two MATCH functions: =INDEX(table, MATCH(row_value, row_headers, 0), MATCH(column_value, column_headers, 0)). Make sure that the ranges used for MATCH are the same size and start in the same place as the INDEX range.

questions.prompt: B2:B7 lists Leeds, Cardiff, Belfast, Bristol, Glasgow, Norwich. What does =MATCH("Belfast",B2:B7,0) return?

options.text: Belfast

questions.hint: MATCH returns a position, and Belfast is the third item.

questions.prompt: With the staff numbers 45, 32, 28, 51, 39, 24 in C2:C7, what does =INDEX(C2:C7,5) return?

options.text: Glasgow

questions.hint: INDEX returns the fifth value in the range.

questions.prompt: Which formula returns the number of staff in Bristol?

options.text: =INDEX(C2:C7,"Bristol")
=MATCH("Bristol",C2:C7,0)
=INDEX(B2:B7,MATCH("Bristol",C2:C7,0))
=INDEX(C2:C7,MATCH("Bristol",B2:B7,0))

questions.hint: MATCH finds the row in the names, and INDEX uses it in the staff column.

questions.prompt: What does =INDEX(B2:C7,3,2) return?

options.text: Belfast

questions.hint: It returns the item in the third row and second column of the block.

questions.prompt: What does =MATCH("Dundee",B2:B7,0) return?

options.text: #REF!
#N/A
#VALUE!

questions.hint: MATCH returns #N/A when the value is not found.

questions.prompt: Why can INDEX and MATCH be better than VLOOKUP when the table changes?

options.text: They return results to the left only
Inserting or deleting columns does not break the formula, as it refers to ranges, not a column number
They automatically update the source data
INDEX and MATCH are faster at sorting data

questions.hint: VLOOKUP's fixed column number can point at the wrong column when the table changes.

questions.prompt: What does a match_type of 0 in MATCH mean?

options.text: Find the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value
Find the smallest value greater than or equal to the lookup value
Ignore case when matching
Find an exact match

questions.hint: Zero requests an exact match, which is the safest in most lookups.

questions.prompt: A MATCH formula omits the third argument. What match type does Excel assume?

options.text: Excel assumes nothing, so it returns an error until a match type is chosen
-1, the smallest value greater than or equal to it
1, the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value
0, an exact match

questions.hint: The default of 1 needs ascending data and can return the wrong row for text IDs.

questions.prompt: For a two-way lookup of a value in a table with row labels and column headings, what is the structure?

options.text: INDEX with a single MATCH for the whole table
VLOOKUP with two lookup values, one for the row and one for the column
MATCH with two INDEX functions
INDEX with one MATCH for the row and another MATCH for the column

questions.hint: Two MATCH functions supply the row and column positions to INDEX.

items.title: L7: Spreadsheets: dates and blanks in COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS
items.body:
Dates in criteria are numbers, so join them to an operator with an ampersand: =COUNTIFS(B2:B6,">="&DATE(2025,3,10),B2:B6,"<"&DATE(2025,3,25)). This counts dates from 10 March up to, but not including, 25 March. Typing ">=10/03/2025" directly may be read in a different way depending on regional settings, so use DATE or a cell reference.

Use the following case data. Column B holds the date received and column C holds the date closed; a blank means the case is still open.
Case 1: received 3 March 2025, closed 12 March. Case 2: received 5 March, still open. Case 3: received 10 March, closed 20 March. Case 4: received 14 March, still open. Case 5: received 18 March, closed 28 March.

To count blanks, use =COUNTBLANK(C2:C6), which returns 2, or =COUNTIFS(C2:C6,""). To count non-blanks, use =COUNTIFS(C2:C6,"<>"), which returns 3. A cell that contains a formula returning "" looks blank but is not truly empty, so COUNTA counts it while COUNTBLANK also counts it. Check carefully when data is produced by formulas.

If you subtract the received date from the closed date for each case, the open cases give a negative number, because a blank counts as zero. Include a test: =IF(C2="","",C2-B2). Then AVERAGE of the result column ignores the text "" cells. The closed cases took 9, 10 and 10 days, so the average is 9.67 days, which displays as 9.7 to one decimal place.

AVERAGEIFS(average_range, criteria_range, criteria) ignores rows that do not meet the criteria. If no row matches, it returns #DIV/0!. Wrap it in IFERROR only when a blank is an acceptable answer, because IFERROR also hides genuine mistakes.

questions.prompt: Using the case data, how many cases were received from 10 March up to but not including 25 March?
questions.hint: Cases 3, 4 and 5 were received on 10, 14 and 18 March.

questions.prompt: Which formula counts those cases correctly?
questions.hint: Join the operator to a DATE function with an ampersand outside the quotation marks.

questions.prompt: What does =COUNTBLANK(C2:C6) return?
questions.hint: Cases 2 and 4 have no closing date.

questions.prompt: What does =COUNTIFS(C2:C6,"<>") return?
questions.hint: The operator <> counts the cells that are not empty.

questions.prompt: Why is =C2-B2 a poor formula for an open case with a blank closing date?

options.text: The blank counts as zero, so the result is a large negative number
It returns zero
It returns today's date
It returns #N/A because a blank cell cannot be used in a subtraction

questions.hint: A blank cell is treated as zero in arithmetic, which makes the answer meaningless.

questions.prompt: Which formula returns the days taken for closed cases and leaves open cases blank?
questions.hint: The test checks for a blank and avoids the subtraction.

questions.prompt: The closed cases took 9, 10 and 10 days. What does the average to one decimal place come to?
questions.hint: 29 days divided by 3 cases is 9.67, or 9.7 to one decimal place.

questions.prompt: What does AVERAGEIFS return if no row meets the criteria?

options.text: #N/A
An empty cell
#DIV/0!

questions.hint: There is nothing to average, so it divides by zero.

questions.prompt: Why should IFERROR be used with care around AVERAGEIFS?

options.text: It only works on text
It changes the criteria used
It slows down every calculation in a large workbook by a noticeable amount
It hides genuine errors as well as the expected one

questions.hint: Masking all errors can leave real mistakes undetected.

items.title: L7: Spreadsheets: pivot tables
items.source: Microsoft Support: create a PivotTable to analyse worksheet data
items.body:
A pivot table summarises a long list of records without writing formulas. You select the data, choose Insert then PivotTable, and drag fields into four areas. Rows list the categories down the left. Columns list categories across the top. Values show the calculation, usually a sum or a count. Filters narrow the whole table to, for example, one year.

The source data should be a clean table: one header row, a single value in each cell, no blank rows or columns, and no merged cells or subtotals. If headers are missing, the pivot table will not work properly.

By default, numbers are summed and text fields are counted. You can change the calculation with Value Field Settings to count, average, maximum, minimum or show values as a percentage of the column total. A pivot table does not update automatically when the source data changes: you must choose Refresh. If you add new rows beyond the original range, convert the source to a table first or change the data source.

Use this data of offices, months and cases: Leeds Jan 40; Leeds Feb 50; Cardiff Jan 30; Cardiff Feb 20; Leeds Jan 10; Bristol Feb 60; Bristol Jan 25; Cardiff Feb 15. Putting Office in rows and Cases in values (sum) gives Leeds 100, Cardiff 65, Bristol 85 and a grand total of 250. Adding Month to columns splits each office into Jan and Feb. The January total is 105 and the February total is 145.

Count of cases in the values area counts rows, so Leeds would show 3 and Bristol 2, not the totals. This is a frequent mistake when a numeric field is accidentally set to Count.

Dates can be grouped by month, quarter or year. A pivot table is a way to explore the data quickly, but check the totals against the source.

questions.prompt: In the data, what total does a pivot table show for Leeds with Office in rows and the sum of Cases in values?
questions.hint: Leeds has rows of 40, 50 and 10.

questions.prompt: What is the grand total of cases in the pivot table?
questions.hint: All eight rows add up to 250.

questions.prompt: A pivot table shows Leeds 3 and Bristol 2, though the cases total over 80 each. What has happened?

options.text: The filter has removed the data
The source data has been sorted in a way that changes the totals shown
The pivot table is showing percentages
The values field has been set to Count rather than Sum

questions.hint: Count tallies rows rather than adding the numbers.

questions.prompt: You add more rows to the source data. What do you need to do for the pivot table to show them?

options.text: Nothing, as pivot tables update automatically
Delete the pivot table and email it again
Sort the source data by date
Refresh the pivot table, and make sure the new rows are within the source range

questions.hint: Pivot tables do not update on their own, and they must include the new rows.

questions.prompt: Which area do you use to show the months across the top of the pivot table?

options.text: Values
Rows
Columns
Filters

questions.hint: Fields in the columns area appear as headings across the top.

questions.prompt: Which feature of a good source table helps the pivot table work properly?

options.text: A subtotal row at the end of each group
A title row above the headings, so the table is easy to identify
Merged cells for each office name
A single header row and no blank rows or merged cells

questions.hint: Clean, consistent data is essential for a reliable summary.

questions.prompt: In the data, what is the total for February?
questions.hint: Feb rows are 50, 20, 60 and 15.

questions.prompt: What does showing values as a percentage of column total do?

options.text: It removes the grand total
It converts the numbers to text so they can no longer be added
It shows each figure as a share of the column's total
It sorts the table in descending order

questions.prompt: A colleague emails a pivot table figure for the monthly report. What is a sensible check?

items.title: L7: Spreadsheets: relative, absolute and mixed references
items.source: Microsoft Support: switch between relative, absolute and mixed references
items.body:
A cell reference changes when you copy a formula, unless you lock it. A relative reference such as B2 shifts: copied one row down it becomes B3, and copied one column right it becomes C2. An absolute reference such as $B$2 never changes, whatever you copy. A mixed reference locks only one part: $B2 locks the column but lets the row move, while B$2 locks the row but lets the column move. Pressing F4 in Excel for Windows cycles through the options when the cursor is in a reference.

A multiplication table shows why mixed references are useful. Put the numbers 2, 3 and 4 in A2:A4 and the numbers 10, 20 and 30 in B1:D1. In B2, type =$A2*B$1 and copy it across to D4. The $A fixes the column of the first number, so every formula multiplies by the value in column A, and the row moves. The B$1 fixes the row of the second number, so every formula multiplies by the value in row 1, and the column moves. The formula in D4 becomes =$A4*D$1, which is 4 times 30, or 120. In B2 the result is 2 times 10, or 20.

A common use is a VAT or inflation rate in one cell, such as $F$1, that every row's formula refers to. If the reference were relative, it would move down and point at an empty cell, giving zero or an error.

When you cut and paste a formula, its references do not change. When you copy it, relative references adjust. When you insert a row inside a range, absolute references adjust to follow the cells they point at.

Check copied formulas by selecting a few cells and reading the formula bar. Use 'Show formulas' on the Formulas tab to see them all at once.

questions.prompt: A multiplication table has 2, 3, 4 in A2:A4 and 10, 20, 30 in B1:D1, with =$A2*B$1 in B2. What does the copied formula in D4 become?
questions.hint: The dollar signs hold column A and row 1, while the other parts move.

questions.hint: D4 is 4 multiplied by 30.

questions.prompt: What does the formula in B4 return (copied from B2)?
questions.hint: B4 is =$A4*B$1, which is 4 times 10.

questions.prompt: In the reference B$2, which part stays fixed when copied?

options.text: The column, but not the row
The row, but not the column
Both the row and column
Neither the row nor column

questions.hint: The dollar before the 2 fixes the row number.

questions.prompt: A rate in F1 is used in a formula in column C that is copied down 50 rows, but the formula returns zero from row 3 onwards. What is the most likely error?

options.text: The formula needs a bracket
The rate cell was formatted as a percentage
The formula was cut and pasted instead of being copied down the column
The reference to F1 was relative and moved down the column

questions.hint: A relative reference slides to F2, F3 and so on, which are empty.

questions.prompt: Which key combination cycles through relative and absolute options in Excel for Windows?

options.text: Ctrl+D
F2
F4
F9

questions.hint: F4 toggles between B2, $B$2, B$2 and $B2 when the cursor is in the reference.

questions.prompt: You cut a cell containing =A1+B1 from C1 and paste it in E5. What happens to the formula?

options.text: It becomes =C5+D5
It returns #REF!
It stays as =A1+B1
It becomes =A5+B5

questions.hint: Cutting and pasting moves the cell without changing its references.

questions.prompt: You copy =A1+B1 from C1 to E5. What does the pasted formula read?
questions.hint: Copying shifts relative references by two columns and four rows.

questions.hint: This displays formulas instead of results so you can check copies.

items.title: L7: Spreadsheets: diagnosing error values
items.source: Microsoft Support: how to correct common formula errors
items.body:
Error values tell you what is wrong. The most common are listed here with their usual cause.

#DIV/0! means a formula divides by zero or by an empty cell, for example =10/0. #VALUE! means the formula contains the wrong type of value, such as adding text to a number: ="abc"+1. #NAME? means Excel does not recognise a name, often a mistyped function such as =SUMM(A1:A3) or text without quotation marks. #REF! means a reference is not valid, typically because a cell, row or column it pointed at has been deleted, or a VLOOKUP column number is bigger than the table. #N/A means a value is not available, and lookup functions return it when nothing is found. #NUM! means a number is invalid, for example =SQRT(-4). A row of hash signs (#####) means the column is too narrow to show the number, or a date or time is negative.

A circular reference occurs when a formula refers to its own cell, directly or through other cells. Excel warns about it and the result may be zero.

IFERROR(value, value_if_error) replaces any error with a result you choose, such as =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A2,F:G,2,FALSE),"Not found"). IFNA does the same for #N/A only. Both should be used with care: IFERROR hides every error, including errors caused by bad data or deleted cells, so a total can look right and be wrong. Prefer IFNA when you only expect missing lookups.

To trace a fault, use Formulas then Evaluate Formula to step through the calculation, and Trace Precedents to see the cells that feed into the formula. Check for numbers stored as text, extra spaces, and ranges that are the wrong size.

Fixing the cause is better than hiding the error. Never overwrite a formula with a typed value to make an error go away.

#VALUE!
#DIV/0!

options.text: #NAME?

options.text: #VALUE!
#NUM!
#DIV/0!
#N/A

questions.hint: A negative number has no real square root, so the number is invalid.

questions.prompt: A formula =SUMM(A1:A3) returns an error. Which one?

options.text: #NAME?
#REF!
#N/A
#VALUE!

questions.hint: Excel does not recognise SUMM as a function.

questions.prompt: A lookup returns #REF! after a colleague deletes a column. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The formula referred to a cell or column that no longer exists
The column is too narrow

questions.hint: Deleted references leave the formula pointing at nothing.

questions.prompt: A cell shows ##### where a number should be. What is the usual fix?

questions.hint: The number is too wide for the column.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between IFERROR and IFNA?

options.text: IFNA replaces only #N/A, while IFERROR replaces every type of error
They do exactly the same thing
IFNA works only on text
IFNA replaces every type of error while IFERROR is limited to #N/A errors only

questions.hint: IFNA is more targeted and so hides fewer genuine mistakes.

questions.prompt: Why is wrapping a large formula in IFERROR(...,0) risky?

options.text: A genuine mistake, like a deleted cell, would show as zero and the total could look correct but be wrong

It prevents the formula being copied

questions.hint: Error values warn you, and hiding them can disguise problems.

questions.prompt: Which tool lets you step through a formula part by part?

options.text: Spelling check

questions.hint: It shows how Excel calculates each part and where the error arises.

items.title: L7: UK GDPR: lawful bases, special category data and roles
items.source: UK GDPR Articles 4, 6, 9, 28 and 35; ICO guidance on lawful basis and DPIAs
items.body:
Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis under Article 6 of the UK GDPR. There are six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Public authorities usually rely on public task, which applies when processing is needed to perform a task in the public interest or an official function with a clear basis in law. Legitimate interests cannot be used by public authorities for tasks they perform as public authorities. Consent is rarely suitable where there is an imbalance of power, because it must be freely given and as easy to withdraw as to give.

Special category data needs extra protection. It covers information on racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data used to identify a person, health, and sex life or sexual orientation. To process it you need both a lawful basis under Article 6 and a separate condition under Article 9. Criminal offence data is dealt with separately under Article 10 and needs official authority or a condition in the Data Protection Act 2018.

A controller decides why and how personal data is processed. A processor handles the data on the controller's behalf and only on its instructions. A written contract is required between them under Article 28. If a supplier decides its own purposes for the data, it becomes a controller in its own right.

A data protection impact assessment, or DPIA, is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people. Examples include large-scale use of special category data, systematic monitoring of a public area and new technologies. The DPIA describes the processing, assesses necessity and risks, and sets out how risks will be reduced. If a high risk remains, you must consult the ICO.

Data minimisation means holding only what is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary.

questions.prompt: Which lawful basis do government departments most often rely on for their core functions?

options.text: Vital interests
Public task
Legitimate interests
Consent

questions.hint: Public task covers processing needed to carry out an official function or task in the public interest.

questions.prompt: Why is consent often an unsuitable lawful basis for a public authority?

options.text: Consent is not allowed under the UK GDPR for any organisation in the public sector
There is an imbalance of power, so consent may not be freely given
Consent only applies to children
Consent can only be given in writing

questions.hint: Valid consent must be freely given and the person must be able to refuse without detriment.

questions.prompt: Which of these is special category data?

options.text: A home address
A date of birth
An employee number
Health information

questions.hint: Health, race, religion, politics, trade union membership and similar topics are special category.

questions.prompt: What does processing special category data require?

options.text: An Article 6 lawful basis and a separate Article 9 condition
Only an Article 6 lawful basis, as special category data has no extra condition
Only an Article 9 condition
The person's written consent in every case

questions.hint: Both a lawful basis and a special category condition are needed.

questions.prompt: A supplier hosts a department's customer database and only acts on the department's instructions. What is the supplier's role?

options.text: Controller
Data subject
Joint controller with the customer
Processor

questions.hint: A processor acts only on the controller's documented instructions.

questions.prompt: What must the department and its processor have in place?

options.text: A letter from the customer
A verbal agreement
A written contract with data protection terms
A copy of the ICO's registration fee receipt

questions.hint: Article 28 requires a binding contract with specific provisions.

questions.prompt: At what point must a DPIA be carried out?

options.text: After a breach has occurred
Only when the ICO asks for one
Before processing likely to result in a high risk to individuals
Whenever personal data is collected, whatever the risk

questions.hint: A DPIA is a preventive assessment of high-risk processing.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of processing that normally needs a DPIA?

options.text: Holding a list of meeting attendees
Updating a staff member's address
Sending a letter to one customer
Large-scale use of health data

questions.hint: Large-scale special category data is a recognised high-risk trigger.

questions.prompt: What does data minimisation mean?

options.text: Deleting all personal data every month, whether or not it is still needed
Holding only the personal data that is adequate, relevant and necessary
Storing data in the smallest possible file
Sharing data only with minors

questions.hint: The principle limits what is collected and kept to what the purpose needs.

items.title: L7: Information requests: FOI, EIR and SARs compared
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000; Environmental Information Regulations 2004; UK GDPR Article 15; ICO guidance
items.body:
Three different regimes deal with requests for information, and the first job is to work out which applies.

A Freedom of Information (FOI) request asks a public authority for recorded information it holds. Anyone can make it, from anywhere, for any reason, and the requester's identity and motive are generally irrelevant. It must be in writing (an email or social media message can count), give a name and an address for reply, and describe the information. The authority must respond within 20 working days. It has a duty to confirm or deny it holds the information and to provide it unless an exemption applies. Some exemptions are absolute, while others require a public interest test. Personal data of other people is often protected by the section 40 exemption. A request can be refused if the cost of finding the information would exceed the appropriate limit (for central government this is £600) or if it is vexatious. Advice and assistance must be offered to help the person to narrow a request.

An Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) request applies to environmental information, such as about land use, emissions or planning. It can be made verbally, and the time limit is also 20 working days.

A subject access request (SAR) is made by a person for their own personal data under the UK GDPR, and the time limit is one calendar month.

If someone asks for their own information through an FOI request, the authority should treat it as a SAR. A request that covers both, such as a request for a department's records of a decision plus the requester's own file, should be separated and handled under the right rules.

The response letter should cite any exemption used, explain the public interest reasoning where it applies, and tell the person about the right to an internal review and to complain to the Information Commissioner.

questions.prompt: A member of the public emails a department asking for the minutes of a policy board. Which regime applies?

options.text: A subject access request
The Environmental Information Regulations
The Data Protection Act 2018 only
Freedom of Information

questions.hint: A request for recorded information held by the authority is normally an FOI request.

questions.prompt: What is the standard FOI response time?

options.text: 40 working days
10 calendar days
One calendar month
20 working days

questions.hint: The FOI Act sets 20 working days from receipt.

options.text: One calendar month
20 working days
30 working days

questions.prompt: What is the position on an FOI requester's reasons for asking?

options.text: They must explain the purpose so the department can weigh the public interest

questions.hint: FOI is applicant blind, with a few exceptions such as vexatious requests.

questions.hint: If it would cost more than the limit to find and extract the information, it may be refused.

questions.hint: The authority has a duty to provide advice and assistance.

items.title: L7: Working remotely and reporting security incidents
items.source: NCSC guidance: home working and 10 steps to cyber security; Government Security Classifications Policy
items.body:
Working from home, on the train or in a cafe changes the risks. Government devices should only be used on networks that are secure. If you need to connect on a public Wi-Fi network, use the approved VPN, which creates an encrypted connection. Never use a personal device to handle OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE information unless your department has approved it, and do not forward work to personal email accounts or cloud storage.

Be aware of the people around you. Shoulder surfing, when someone watches your screen or listens to a call, is a real risk in public places. Position your screen away from view, consider a privacy filter and avoid discussing sensitive work. At home, lock your screen when you leave the device, even if family members are around. Store paper and laptops securely, and never leave a device in a car.

Do not plug in unknown USB sticks, for instance one found in a car park, because they can carry malware. Removable media should be approved and encrypted, and used only if there is a business reason.

Multi-factor authentication adds a second check to a password, such as a code from an app, and protects an account even if the password is stolen. Keep software updated as updates fix known weaknesses.

If something goes wrong, report it at once. A security incident can be a lost or stolen laptop or phone, an email sent to the wrong person, a suspected phishing click, or a suspicious request for access. Report to your security team or the contact set out in your department's guidance, even if you think the device is encrypted or the harm is small. Early reporting lets the team lock accounts, wipe devices and meet legal deadlines, such as notifying the ICO within 72 hours when required. Do not try to fix a problem alone or hide it.

A culture of reporting without blame helps people to report quickly. Honest mistakes should be learned from.

options.text: Share your hotspot with the person next to you

questions.hint: A VPN encrypts the connection and reduces the risk of interception.

questions.hint: Quick action limits the damage and lets the team check for compromise.

items.title: L7: Reading data: weighted averages, shares and indices
items.source: Office for National Statistics: guide to index numbers; Government Analysis Function guidance on communicating statistics
items.body:
Not every average is a simple one. A weighted average gives more influence to groups with more cases. Suppose Region A handles 200 cases and succeeds in 90 per cent, while Region B handles 800 and succeeds in 70 per cent. The simple average of the two percentages is 80 per cent, but that treats the regions as equal. The weighted average is (200 x 0.90 + 800 x 0.70) divided by 1,000, which is 74 per cent. Because Region B is four times the size, the overall result is much closer to its rate. This is why you should not average percentages without checking the group sizes.

A share is a part divided by the whole. If one team handles 45 of 180 cases, its share is 45 divided by 180, or 25 per cent. Check that shares add to 100 per cent, allowing for rounding.

An index sets a starting value to 100 so that changes are easier to compare. If a measure is 50 in 2020 and 65 in 2024, the 2024 index is 65 divided by 50 times 100, which is 130. This means the measure is 30 per cent higher than in the base year. Indices are useful for comparing items measured in different units.

Be careful with small numbers. A rise from 2 to 4 cases is a 100 per cent increase but is only 2 cases, and may be random variation. Give the actual numbers alongside percentages. Beware of comparing groups of different sizes by using counts rather than rates.

Sampling matters: a survey of a few hundred people gives an estimate with a margin of error, not an exact figure. A biased sample, for example a survey that only reaches online users, can give misleading results.

State the source, the date and any definitions or changes to them.

questions.prompt: Region A handles 200 cases at a 90% success rate and Region B handles 800 cases at 70%. What is the overall success rate?
questions.hint: The weighted average is (180 + 560) / 1,000.

questions.prompt: Why is the simple average of 90% and 70% misleading in this case?

options.text: It cannot be calculated with percentages unless the group sizes are equal
It treats the two regions as equal even though one is four times larger
It is always lower than the weighted average
It ignores the higher figure

questions.hint: The larger region should have more influence on the overall result.

questions.prompt: One team handled 45 out of 180 cases. What is its share?
questions.hint: 45 divided by 180 is 0.25.

questions.prompt: A measure is 50 in 2020 and 65 in 2024. What is the 2024 index with 2020 as 100?

The measure is 130% higher than in the base year
The measure has risen by 130 units

questions.hint: An index of 130 means 30 per cent above the base.

questions.hint: Small numbers can fluctuate randomly, so give actual counts.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to compare two regions using rates rather than counts?

options.text: Rates adjust for the size of each region
Rates are always larger than counts
Counts cannot be added
Rates avoid the need for a source

questions.hint: A larger region will have more cases simply because it has more people.

As the exact satisfaction of all customers
As unreliable and not worth using
As a census

questions.hint: Sample results are estimates of a wider population.

questions.prompt: An online-only survey is used to judge satisfaction among all claimants. What is the main concern?
